Hi! Thanks for bringing up the discussion. In our setup, we adopt a unified evaluation framework where the entire time series is used as test data, and the initial portion of the time series—assumed to be normal or containing a minimal number of anomalies—serves as the training data for semi-supervised methodologies.

The fundamental assumption of semi-supervised approaches, which require training data, is to learn normal patterns from the training dataset and subsequently identify abnormal instances across the entire time series. To achieve this, we assume the initial segment of the time series is either anomaly-free or contains a minimal number of anomalies. However, not all datasets in our collection come pre-split into train/test sets, which provides us the opportunity to recommend a standardized setup.

Specifically, we use the smaller value between the index of the first anomaly and the initial 25% of the time series as the training set across our benchmarking practice. Nevertheless, some datasets present edge cases where the first anomaly appears very early, potentially leading to underfitting issues for learning-based approaches. To mitigate this, we impose a minimum training data length of 500 time steps. In summary, the entire time series is consistently employed as test data, while the initial segment serves as the training data under our unified framework.

Let us know any questions you might have and we are happy to discuss more.
